title: The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson
author: Mark Twain
setting: Dawson’s Landing, a slaveholding river town on the Missouri bank of the Mississippi, from 1830 to the early 1850s
lengthNote: A short novel: ‘A Whisper to the Reader’, twenty-one chapters and a Conclusion, each chapter headed by maxims from Pudd’nhead Wilson’s Calendar
openingLine: The scene of this chronicle is the town of Dawson’s Landing, on the Missouri side of the Mississippi, half a day’s journey, per steamboat, below St. Louis.
summary: An enslaved nurse who is one-sixteenth Black, and looks white, swaps her infant son with her master’s, so that her child is raised as the heir and the heir as a slave. Twenty-three years later the changeling murders his supposed uncle, and the town’s despised lawyer proves who did it, and who everyone really is, from the fingerprints he has been collecting on glass for two decades as a hobby. Twain calls it a tragedy and means it: the science that solves the crime also returns the innocent man to a life he cannot live and sends the guilty one, as property, down the river.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson
sourceText.note: References give the chapter number as the book numbers them; the last chapter is headed ‘Conclusion’. The novel’s dialogue repeatedly uses a racial slur, and the passages quoted here have been chosen so as not to reproduce it.

atAGlance.label: Serialised
atAGlance.note: Seven instalments in The Century Magazine, while Twain’s publishing firm was sliding towards bankruptcy.

atAGlance.label: First book editions
atAGlance.note: Chatto & Windus in London; the American Publishing Company of Hartford in November, bound together with the farce it grew out of, Those Extraordinary Twins.

atAGlance.label: Where written
atAGlance.note: Twain drafted it in Italy in 1892–93, and the Whisper to the Reader is dated from a villa outside the city.

atAGlance.label: Time span
atAGlance.note: Two babies born on 1 February 1830; the murder and the trial come twenty-three years later, before the Civil War.

atAGlance.label: The evidence
atAGlance.note: Wilson has been taking ‘finger-marks’ on glass since the year of the twins’ birth. Francis Galton’s Finger Prints appeared in 1892, while Twain was writing.

structure.label: Whisper and Chapters 1–2
structure.title: A town, a joke, and a threat of the river
structure.summary: Dawson’s Landing is introduced house by house, with its cats and its First Families of Virginia. David Wilson arrives in 1830, makes a remark about wishing he owned half of a dog, and is named Pudd’nhead for the next twenty years. Percy Driscoll, robbed of small change, threatens to sell his four house slaves down the river, and Roxy, holding two babies who look alike, hears the sentence that will decide the book.

scenes.title: Half a dog
scenes.summary: Wilson’s joke is examined by the citizens with the care of a court, and found to be idiocy.

scenes.title: The one minute
scenes.summary: Driscoll takes out his watch; three slaves confess to a theft; he sells them locally and writes up his mercy in his diary.

structure.label: Chapters 3–4
structure.title: Roxy changes the babies
structure.summary: Terrified that her son might one day be sold south, Roxy first plans to drown them both and then, dressing each child in the other’s clothes, swaps them in their cradles. She reasons her way to it through a sermon on free grace and the example of kings. Chapter 4 follows the changelings growing up: the false Tom petted and vicious, the real heir, now ‘Chambers’, learning to take blows and to protect the boy who deals them.

scenes.title: The cradles
scenes.summary: Roxy argues herself from despair into a plan, and only Wilson, taking the babies’ finger-marks, sees them both before and after.

scenes.title: The changelings
scenes.summary: Tom grows up cruel and Chambers grows up his bodyguard; Roxy watches her own son learn to despise her.

structure.label: Chapters 5–7
structure.title: The Italian twins arrive
structure.summary: Luigi and Angelo Capello, travelling Italian nobles, take lodgings with Aunt Patsy Cooper and are received by the town as visiting royalty. Their arrival gives Dawson’s Landing something to look at and gives Tom, home from Yale with debts and a taste for gambling, someone to resent. Judge Driscoll shows the twins Wilson’s Calendar, and the town laughs at it.

scenes.title: The letter
scenes.summary: Aunt Patsy’s advertisement is answered by two twins who will pay for two.

scenes.title: The reception
scenes.summary: The whole town shakes hands with the Counts.

scenes.title: The unknown nymph
scenes.summary: Wilson sees a young woman practising attitudes in Tom’s bedroom window, and cannot account for her.

structure.label: Chapters 8–10
structure.title: Roxy comes home and tells Tom what he is
structure.summary: Freed, ruined by a failed bank and crippled by rheumatism, Roxy comes back expecting a dollar a month from the son she made a gentleman. He kicks the real heir out of the room and refuses her, and she turns from supplicant to judge in a single speech. In the haunted house she tells him he is her son and a slave, and the rest of the book runs on that knowledge: Tom pays her half his allowance, learns he cannot shake hands, and finds that his character has not changed at all.

scenes.title: The dollar
scenes.summary: Tom refuses his old nurse a dollar; she tells him he has had his chance and trampled it.

scenes.title: The haunted house
scenes.summary: Roxy names him Valet de Chambers and takes half his pension; he asks who his father was.

scenes.title: The moral landscape
scenes.summary: A week of horror, then the old Tom resurfaces; he raids the town in a girl’s dress.

structure.label: Chapters 11–14
structure.title: A palm, a kick and a duel refused
structure.summary: Wilson reads Luigi’s palm and finds a killing in it. Tom baits Luigi at a public meeting and is kicked across the stage; instead of challenging him he takes him to court, and Judge Driscoll, hearing that blood of his race has crawled to the law, tears up his will and fights the duel himself. Roxy, told that her son declined to fight, disowns the ‘one part’ of him that is her own.

scenes.title: The palm
scenes.summary: Tom mocks Wilson’s finger-marks and palmistry; Wilson reads in Luigi’s hand that he has killed someone.

scenes.title: The shame of Judge Driscoll
scenes.summary: The Judge learns that Tom sued rather than fought, and destroys the will.

scenes.title: Roxana insists upon reform
scenes.summary: Roxy tells Tom that only his soul is the part of him that is Black, and it is not worth saving.

structure.label: Chapters 15–16
structure.title: The robber robbed, and a mother sold
structure.summary: Tom’s stolen goods, including the twins’ jewelled dagger, cannot be pawned because the town has been warned. Roxy offers to be sold to clear his debts, on condition that he sells her upstate and buys her back within a year; he forges a bill of sale and sells her to an Arkansas cotton planter instead. She learns the truth from the current of the river.

scenes.title: The dagger
scenes.summary: Wilson and the constable joke about the stoop-shouldered old woman who raided the town.

scenes.title: The paddle-box
scenes.summary: Roxy, on the lower guard of the boat, sees the water running the wrong way.

structure.label: Chapters 17–19
structure.title: Roxy escapes, and Tom kills the Judge
structure.summary: Roxy escapes the plantation, reaches St. Louis and confronts Tom with what he has done; she orders him to raise the money to buy her free. He goes to rob his uncle’s safe in a girl’s clothes and blacked face, and when the old man wakes he kills him with the Indian dagger stolen from the twins. Luigi and Angelo, out walking, find the body and are arrested.

scenes.title: Roxana commands
scenes.summary: Roxy tells the story of her escape and takes charge of her son’s finances again.

scenes.title: The knife
scenes.summary: The Judge stirs in his sleep; Tom strikes and runs; the twins are found standing over the body.

structure.label: Chapters 20–22
structure.title: The trial, and what the fingerprints prove
structure.summary: Wilson, defending the twins, has nothing until Tom idly presses a finger to one of his glass strips and Wilson recognises the mark on the knife. Overnight he enlarges his records with a pantograph and in court proves first that the murderer is Tom and then, from prints taken in 1830, that Tom is not Tom. The Conclusion returns each man to his legal category: the real heir cannot bear the parlour, and the false one, now a slave, is pardoned in order to be sold.

scenes.title: The glass strip
scenes.summary: Tom leaves his fingerprint on Wilson’s glass and Wilson sees the assassin’s signature.

scenes.title: Doom
scenes.summary: A and B, five months and seven months; the courtroom watches two babies exchange names.

scenes.title: The creditors
scenes.summary: Tom is inventoried as property and sold; the town elects itself pudd’nhead.

characters.name: Roxana (Roxy)
characters.role: Enslaved nurse to both babies, later free, later sold
characters.summary: One-sixteenth Black, and so a slave, she is the only person in the book who acts on the arithmetic the town lives by. She swaps the babies out of terror, is despised for twenty years by the son she made a gentleman, and then rules him, bargains with him and is betrayed by him. Twain gives her the grandest bearing in the novel and the most exact understanding of what everyone in it is worth.
characters.clue: She dresses one baby in the other’s clothes and spends the rest of her life ruled, and finally sold, by the result.

relationships.label: mother of, and later blackmailer and victim of
relationships.note: He is her son by Colonel Essex; she makes him white and he sells her.

relationships.label: raised as her son the boy she robbed

characters.name: ‘Tom’ Driscoll (Valet de Chambre)
characters.role: Roxy’s son, raised as Percy Driscoll’s heir
characters.summary: Petted, cowardly, a gambler and a thief in a girl’s dress, he is the book’s villain and also its experiment: the reader is invited to ask whether he is what he is because of ‘training’ or because of his blood, and Twain plants evidence for both. Told the truth of his birth he feels his hand hang limp instead of offering a handshake, and within a week is himself again.
characters.clue: Raised as the heir, he learns in a haunted house that he is a slave, pays his mother half his allowance to keep quiet, and then sells her.

relationships.label: son of, then master and seller of

characters.name: ‘Chambers’ (the real Tom Driscoll)
characters.role: Percy Driscoll’s son, raised as a slave
characters.summary: He has almost no lines and no inner life on the page, which is the point: he is what the exchange left over. He fights Tom’s battles, saves him from drowning and is kicked for it, and when the trial makes him rich and white he can neither read nor sit in the parlour. His fate is the last thing the book refuses to follow.
characters.clue: Born the heir, he is the household’s errand boy and bodyguard until a courtroom makes him a gentleman he has no idea how to be.

characters.name: David ‘Pudd’nhead’ Wilson
characters.role: Lawyer without a case, collector of finger-marks
characters.summary: A joke about a dog costs him twenty years of practice, and he spends them on accountancy, a whimsical almanac and glass strips smeared with the town’s fingers. He is patient, decent and a little dull, and the novel makes him a detective almost by accident: the evidence was in his cabinet all along, waiting for someone to press a thumb on a glass.
characters.clue: He wishes he owned half a dog so that he could kill his half, and the town takes twenty years to see the joke.

characters.name: Judge York Leicester Driscoll
characters.role: First citizen of Dawson’s Landing, Tom’s supposed uncle
characters.summary: A freethinker whose only religion is to be a gentleman without stain, he judges the county and lives by the Virginia code. He forgives Tom’s debts and remakes his will twice, and the one thing he cannot forgive is a Driscoll taking a blow to court. He fights the duel his nephew refused, and is killed in his sleep for the contents of his safe.
characters.clue: His only religion is to be a gentleman without stain, and he tears up his will when he hears that his nephew went to law instead of to the field.

relationships.label: fights a duel with, then campaigns against

characters.name: Percy Northumberland Driscoll
characters.role: The Judge’s younger brother, father of the real Tom, Roxy’s owner
characters.summary: A speculator who leaves the nursery to Roxy and is proud of his mercy when he sells three slaves locally rather than down the river. The threat he makes with his watch in his hand is the engine of the plot, and he dies in Chapter 4 without ever suspecting which child is his.
characters.clue: He gives his slaves one minute by his watch to confess, and records his own clemency in his diary that night.

characters.name: Luigi and Angelo Capello
characters.role: Italian twins lodging with Aunt Patsy Cooper
characters.summary: Left over from the farce Twain separated out of the novel, they are handsome, musical and faintly implausible, and the town adores them until it is convenient to hang them. Luigi has killed a man to save his brother; the dagger he did it with is stolen by Tom and used on the Judge, which puts the twins at the murder scene with the weapon and no alibi.
characters.clue: Two travelling counts who play four-handed piano, are elected to a temperance society by mistake, and end up on trial for a murder committed with their own knife.

relationships.label: fight a duel with, then are ruined by

characters.name: Pembroke Howard
characters.role: Lawyer, the Judge’s friend and second, public prosecutor at the trial
characters.summary: The town’s authority on the duelling code, ready to explain any doubtful act with any weapon from bradawls to artillery. He seconds the Judge against Luigi and prosecutes the twins for his murder, which means that in the last chapters the code of honour and the law of Missouri are being argued by the same man.
characters.clue: An authority on the ‘code’, he will meet you in the field with any weapon from bradawls to artillery, and later prosecutes the men he saw duel with his friend.

themes.name: Race as a fiction of law
themes.summary: Roxy is white to every sense and a slave by arithmetic, and the novel keeps the sum in view: one part in sixteen ‘outvoted’ the other fifteen. Because the babies are told apart only by their clothes, the book can test what race is made of by swapping the clothes, and the answer it gives is that race is whatever the town has decided to see. Twain never lets the reader forget that the decision is enforced with a bill of sale.
themes.development: Stated as a fact of law in Chapter 2, felt as a change in Tom’s body in Chapter 10, and enforced by the creditors in the Conclusion.

themes.name: Property in persons
themes.summary: Every human relationship in the book has a price attached, and the plot is a series of transactions: a child exchanged, an allowance halved, a mother sold for six hundred dollars, a murderer inventoried. The last page settles the question of Tom’s guilt by asking who owns him, and the town finds the answer reasonable.
themes.development: Percy Driscoll’s watch in Chapter 2 sets the terms; Tom recognises himself as ‘chattel’ in Chapter 10; the Conclusion applies the rule to him.

themes.name: Nature and nurture
themes.summary: The peach was once a bitter almond, says the Calendar, and the exchanged children look like proof that training is everything. But Twain complicates his own experiment: Tom is vicious before he can talk, and Roxy blames his cowardice on the one part of him that is hers. The book offers evidence on both sides and refuses to total it.
themes.development: The maxim heads Chapter 5, after Chapter 4 has shown a bad baby and a good one; Chapter 10 claims a moral landslide and then reports that nothing moved.

themes.name: The Virginia code
themes.summary: The First Families live by unwritten laws as strict as statute, and the duel is their court. Judge Driscoll would rather lose a nephew than see one go to law over a kick, and the code is presented with real admiration and complete absurdity at once: it is the one thing in Dawson’s Landing that is not for sale, and it gets its keeper killed.
themes.development: Set out as the town’s aristocracy in Chapter 1, tested by Tom’s lawsuit in Chapter 12, and taken over by Roxy, who despises cowardice as fiercely as the Judge does, in Chapter 14.

themes.name: Evidence and the signature of the body
themes.summary: Wilson’s glass strips turn the body into a document that cannot be forged, and the trial is the first fiction to hang a case on fingerprints. The book is careful about what they prove: they identify the hand, and the town then attaches to that hand a name, a race and a legal status the prints know nothing about.
themes.development: Introduced as a hobby in Chapter 1, mocked in Chapter 11, and turned into a courtroom method with a pantograph in Chapter 21.

themes.name: Reputation and the name Pudd’nhead
themes.summary: One remark fixes Wilson’s standing for twenty years, and the town’s judgment is shown as a machine that runs on itself: no new evidence can reach it until a courtroom produces something it cannot laugh at. Roxy’s standing turns on the same hinge in reverse, from marvel of the kitchens to a woman with a bill of sale in her pocket.
themes.development: The name is conferred in Chapter 1, defended by the Judge in Chapter 5, and resigned in the Conclusion, when the town elects itself to the vacancy.

techniques.name: Epigram
techniques.definition: A short balanced sentence that sounds like settled wisdom and usually turns a received idea inside out.
techniques.inThisBook: Each chapter opens with maxims from Pudd’nhead Wilson’s Calendar, the almanac that convinced the town he was a fool; they comment on the chapter obliquely and give the narrator a voice colder than the story’s.

techniques.name: Dialect
techniques.definition: Spelling and grammar used to mark where a speaker comes from, and what being heard that way costs them.
techniques.inThisBook: Roxy’s speech is the book’s richest instrument, and the plot depends on it: the real heir, raised in the kitchen, ends the novel unable to speak in the parlour.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The audience knows something a character on stage does not.
techniques.inThisBook: From Chapter 3 the reader knows which baby is which, so every scene in which the Judge indulges his ‘nephew’ or Tom cuffs his ‘slave’ is read twice.

techniques.name: Disguise
techniques.definition: A character concealing their identity, so that the audience knows more than the people on stage do.
techniques.inThisBook: Tom robs the town as a girl and as an old woman and kills in blackface; the disguises are literal versions of the one he has worn since the cradle.

techniques.name: Identical twins
techniques.definition: Two people who cannot be told apart, used to test what identity consists of.
techniques.inThisBook: The Capellos are the visible pair; the invisible pair are Tom and Chambers, identical in the cradle and separated by a change of clothes.

techniques.name: Names that argue
techniques.definition: Names chosen so that the name itself makes a claim about the person or the world.
techniques.inThisBook: Roxy calls her son Valet de Chambre because it sounds grand; ‘Thomas à Becket’ and ‘Percy Northumberland’ carry England’s aristocracy into a river town; and ‘Pudd’nhead’ is a name the town gives and the title Twain keeps.

quotations.context: The first maxim from Pudd’nhead Wilson’s Calendar, heading the first chapter.
quotations.analysis: The Calendar begins by dropping honesty to the level of a card-table tactic, and the sentence is built like a hand of whist: two options, one object. It is a warning about the narrator as much as the town, since the book that follows will tell the truth and trump in about equal measure.
quotations.text: Tell the truth or trump⁠—but get the trick.

quotations.context: Wilson’s first remark in Dawson’s Landing, provoked by an invisible dog that will not stop howling.
quotations.analysis: The joke is about property in a living creature, which is the subject of the whole novel: the citizens who dissect it for a page, wondering what would become of the other half, are reasoning about a dog exactly as they reason about people. Twain lets the town convict Wilson of idiocy for saying out loud what its own institutions assume.
quotations.text: I wish I owned half of that dog.

quotations.context: The narrator introducing Judge Driscoll, the town’s chief citizen.
quotations.analysis: The dash and the repetition make ‘gentleman’ the article of faith and ‘without stain or blemish’ the creed, in a sentence that also tells us the Judge is a freethinker. The book will take him at his word: the stain he cannot live with is not murder or slavery but a nephew who went to court.
quotations.text: To be a gentleman⁠—a gentleman without stain or blemish⁠—was his only religion, and to it he was always faithful.

quotations.context: The Calendar maxim that heads the chapter in which Percy Driscoll spares his slaves.
quotations.analysis: The maxim turns the Fall into a joke about prohibition, and the chapter beneath it is entirely about the power to forbid. Read after the chapter, the apple that is wanted only because it is forbidden looks like the sugar and the small change the house slaves take from a master who could sell them for it.
quotations.text: Adam was but human⁠—this explains it all. He did not want the apple for the apple’s sake, he wanted it only because it was forbidden.

quotations.context: The narrator describing Roxy and her baby, before the exchange.
quotations.analysis: The verb is ‘outvoted’, which makes racial classification an election in which fifteen parts lose to one, and ‘a fiction of law and custom’ names the mechanism without raising the voice. The sentence about the child follows without a paragraph break, so that his status is derived from his mother’s by the same arithmetic in the same breath.
quotations.text: To all intents and purposes Roxy was as white as anybody, but the one sixteenth of her which was black outvoted the other fifteen parts and made her a Negro. She was a slave, and salable as such. Her child was thirty-one parts white, and he, too, was a slave, and by a fiction of law and custom a Negro.

quotations.context: Percy Driscoll, watch in hand, to his four house slaves after a theft.
quotations.analysis: The dash before the final clause is a pause for effect, and the effect is theological: the narrator says at once that the phrase was equivalent to a sentence of hell. The threat is never carried out on the people it is made to, and lands instead on the baby in the room, who will be sold down the river on the last page.
quotations.text: If at the end of that time you have not confessed, I will not only sell all four of you, but⁠—I will sell you down the river!

quotations.context: The Calendar maxim that heads the chapter in which Roxy exchanges the children.
quotations.analysis: The sentence sets up a hymn of gratitude and pays it off with death, and the chapter it introduces is one in which a mother decides that killing her child would be a mercy. The Calendar’s habit of praising the wrong benefactor prepares the reader for a plot in which every good turn is a form of harm.
quotations.text: Whoever has lived long enough to find out what life is, knows how deep a debt of gratitude we owe to Adam, the first great benefactor of our race. He brought death into the world.

quotations.context: Roxy, alone with the two babies, arguing herself towards the exchange.
quotations.analysis: She reaches for precedent, as a lawyer would, and finds it in a sermon about an English queen’s child swapped in the cradle. The repetition of ‘no sin’ is the sound of a conscience being talked round, and the precedent she settles on is royalty: the book’s changeling plot is announced as an aristocratic tradition.
quotations.text: ’Tain’t no sin⁠—white folks has done it! It ain’t no sin, glory to goodness it ain’t no sin! Dey’s done it⁠—yes, en dey was de biggest quality in de whole bilin’, too⁠—kings!

quotations.context: The Calendar maxim heading the chapter in which the twins arrive, immediately after the chapter on the changelings’ upbringing.
quotations.analysis: Placed straight after Chapter 4, the maxim reads as a verdict on Tom and Chambers, and its examples are both improvements by cultivation. The joke about a college education is aimed at Tom, who has just come back from Yale no better than he went, so the Calendar contradicts the chapter it heads in the act of summarising it.
quotations.text: Training is everything. The peach was once a bitter almond; cauliflower is nothing but cabbage with a college education.

quotations.context: Chambers, the real heir, teasing Roxy in Judge Driscoll’s kitchen.
quotations.analysis: The boy who is white by birth calls himself imitation white, and neither speaker knows how exactly wrong and right he is. The word ‘imitation’ runs through the scene as a joke about complexion and comes out as the book’s definition of race: a category of performance, judged by the audience.
quotations.text: Bofe of us is imitation white⁠—dat’s what we is⁠—en pow’ful good imitation, too

quotations.context: Roxy, refused a dollar by her son, rising from supplication to judgement.
quotations.analysis: The tense changes do the work: three perfect tenses of what he has done, then a future in which he kneels. The narrator has just described her frame straightening as she speaks, and the prophecy is fulfilled within the chapter, which makes this the moment the plot passes from the white household to the woman it owns.
quotations.text: You has said de word. You has had yo’ chance, en you has trompled it under yo’ foot. When you git another one, you’ll git down on yo’ knees en beg for it!

quotations.context: Roxy to Tom in the haunted house, before telling him whose son he is.
quotations.analysis: She makes the revelation in two steps, and this first one is a puzzle: it withdraws the Driscoll blood without yet saying what replaces it. ‘Den I is’ is the trap, since the listener assumes she is kin to nobody, and the narrator has just compared her to a Fate.
quotations.text: You ain’t no more kin to ole Marse Driscoll den I is!

quotations.context: Tom, days after learning his birth, thinking about his uncle the Judge.
quotations.analysis: Four nouns for himself, each more inanimate than the last, and then the comparison with the dog that Wilson wanted to own half of in Chapter 1. The sentence is the first time the false heir has understood the institution he has lived on, and the understanding arrives as hatred of his benefactor rather than of the institution.
quotations.text: He is white; and I am his chattel, his property, his goods, and he can sell me, just as he could his dog.

quotations.context: Judge Driscoll on learning that Tom sued Luigi for assault instead of challenging him.
quotations.analysis: Three insults in descending order of size, cur to scum to vermin, before the sentence that names the offence: ‘crawled to a court of law’. The Judge is himself a judge, and the code he serves ranks the law he administers below the duel; Twain gives the contradiction to the most honourable man in the book.
quotations.text: You cur! You scum! You vermin! Do you mean to tell me that blood of my race has suffered a blow and crawled to a court of law about it?

quotations.context: The Calendar maxim heading the chapter in which Tom, disinherited, stares at ruin.
quotations.analysis: The list arrives out of calendar order and includes every month, so that the caution in the first sentence is cancelled by the second. Under it sits a chapter about a gambler whose speculations have just cost him a will, and the maxim mimics his reasoning: a rule that sounds prudent and forbids nothing.
quotations.text: October. This is one of the peculiarly dangerous months to speculate in stocks in. The others are July, January, September, April, November, May, March, June, December, August, and February.

quotations.context: The Calendar maxim heading the chapter in which Tom sells his mother.
quotations.analysis: The maxim is placed above the book’s cruellest act, and it fits with a click: Roxy picked up a child and made him prosperous, and he bites. It is also the third dog in the novel, after Wilson’s half-dog and Tom’s ‘just as he could his dog’, and the comparison has moved from property to gratitude.
quotations.text: If you pick up a starving dog and make him prosperous, he will not bite you. This is the principal difference between a dog and a man.

quotations.context: Roxy on the steamboat, the moment she reads the current and understands which way she is travelling.
quotations.analysis: She discovers the betrayal not from a person but from the water, because she has been a chambermaid on these boats for years and knows what a snag’s ‘break’ means. The phrase she uses is the one Percy Driscoll used in Chapter 2 as a threat; it has taken fourteen chapters to reach the person who feared it most.
quotations.text: Oh, de good Lord God have mercy on po’ sinful me⁠—I’s sole down de river!

quotations.context: The Calendar maxim heading the chapter in which the Judge is murdered.
quotations.analysis: The chapter beneath it is the killing of a man who has been a good example to his nephew for twenty years, and the maxim is spoken in the voice of the nephew. The Calendar’s trick, here as elsewhere, is to be funny in the abstract and appalling once the chapter has been read.
quotations.text: Few things are harder to put up with than the annoyance of a good example.

quotations.context: The Calendar maxim heading the chapter in which the trial of the twins opens.
quotations.analysis: The warning is aimed at the case Pembroke Howard is about to make from the dagger and the twins’ presence at the body, and it is followed by an example about a pencil that proves the point by being ridiculous. Wilson’s fingerprints will win the trial precisely because they are not circumstantial: they are the murderer’s own signature.
quotations.text: Even the clearest and most perfect circumstantial evidence is likely to be at fault, after all, and therefore ought to be received with great caution.

quotations.context: Wilson opening his argument to the court before introducing the fingerprint evidence.
quotations.analysis: He calls the print a signature and an autograph, words for a mark a person makes deliberately, and then describes a mark the body makes without consent. The speech turns the human being into a document that carries its own proof of identity, and the novel immediately shows what a town does with such a document: it reads a race and a legal status into it.
quotations.text: Every human being carries with him from his cradle to his grave certain physical marks which do not change their character, and by which he can always be identified⁠—and that without shade of doubt or question. These marks are his signature, his physiological autograph, so to speak

quotations.context: Wilson to Tom, in open court, after matching his childhood print to the mark on the knife.
quotations.analysis: The sentence restores Tom’s birth name, his legal category and his crime in one breath, and the order matters: he is named as a slave before he is named as a murderer. The command to make the prints on the window is never obeyed, because he faints, and the narrator says there is no need. The body has already confessed.
quotations.text: Valet de Chambre, Negro and slave⁠—falsely called Thomas à Becket Driscoll⁠—make upon the window the fingerprints that will hang you!

quotations.context: The second Calendar maxim heading the Conclusion.
quotations.analysis: A date and a discovery, and then the wish that it had not happened: it is the last thing the Calendar says, and it sits above the page on which America sells a man to satisfy his late owner’s creditors. Wilson’s almanac has spent the novel being mistaken for foolishness, and its final entry is the book’s judgment on the country it is set in.
quotations.text: October 12, the Discovery. It was wonderful to find America, but it would have been more wonderful to miss it.

quotations.context: The narrator on what the verdict does to the man who was raised as Chambers.
quotations.analysis: ‘Rich and free’ is followed at once by ‘embarrassing’, a word too small for the situation and chosen for that reason. The list that follows is an inventory of a body trained for one place, and it is the novel’s answer to the Calendar’s claim that training is everything: training is everything, and it cannot be undone by a verdict.
quotations.text: The real heir suddenly found himself rich and free, but in a most embarrassing situation. He could neither read nor write, and his speech was the basest dialect of the Negro quarter. His gait, his attitudes, his gestures, his bearing, his laugh⁠—all were vulgar and uncouth; his manners were the manners of a slave.

quotations.context: The last sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The pardon and the sale share a sentence, joined by ‘and’, as though one followed from the other, which in the town’s reasoning it does: a valuable slave cannot be wasted in prison. The threat Percy Driscoll made with his watch in Chapter 2 is carried out on his brother’s murderer, and the book ends on the phrase it began with.
quotations.text: As soon as the Governor understood the case, he pardoned Tom at once, and the creditors sold him down the river.

timeline.label: The Missouri Compromise
timeline.detail: Missouri enters the Union as a slave state, which makes Dawson’s Landing a slaveholding town on a river that divides free soil from slave.

timeline.label: The novel’s two babies are born
timeline.detail: On 1 February, in Percy Driscoll’s house; David Wilson arrives in the town the same month.

timeline.label: Samuel Clemens born in Florida, Missouri
timeline.detail: He grows up in Hannibal, a river town the book’s Dawson’s Landing closely resembles.

timeline.label: The Dred Scott decision
timeline.detail: The Supreme Court rules that people of African descent cannot be citizens, the legal world in which Tom is ‘inventoried’.

timeline.label: The Thirteenth Amendment abolishes slavery
timeline.detail: Twain writes the novel a generation later, looking back at an institution the law had ended and the country had not.

timeline.label: Francis Galton publishes Finger Prints
timeline.detail: The first systematic account of fingerprints as a means of identification, appearing while Twain was at work on the novel.

timeline.label: Serialisation begins in The Century Magazine
timeline.detail: December 1893 to June 1894; the farce about the twins had been separated out of the story during composition.

timeline.label: Twain’s publishing firm fails
timeline.detail: Charles L. Webster & Company goes bankrupt in April, the money trouble that shadowed the writing of the book.

timeline.label: First book editions
timeline.detail: Chatto & Windus in London; the American Publishing Company of Hartford in November, with Those Extraordinary Twins appended.

timeline.label: Plessy v. Ferguson
timeline.detail: The Supreme Court upholds racial segregation, two years after a novel about a woman who is white in every respect but law.

places.name: Hannibal, Missouri
places.note: The river town of Twain’s boyhood, and the model for Dawson’s Landing, half a day below St. Louis by steamboat.

places.name: St. Louis
places.note: Where Tom gambles, where Roxy escapes to, and where he sells her.

places.name: New Orleans
places.note: The far end of the river and of the book’s worst threat; Roxy banks her wages there and loses them.

places.name: Cairo, Illinois
places.note: Where Roxy takes the local packet home on her return in Chapter 8.

places.name: Florence
places.note: Where Twain wrote the novel in 1892–93, and from which the Whisper to the Reader is dated.

criticalViews.position: A novel about the invention of race
criticalViews.summary: The most influential modern reading treats the exchange of babies as a controlled experiment: since nothing but clothing distinguishes the children, whatever the town later sees in them is what the town has put there, and the book exposes race as a legal fiction maintained by force.
criticalViews.counter: Twain’s narrator sometimes talks as if blood were real, and Roxy blames her son’s cowardice on the ‘one part’ that is hers; the book does not always agree with the reading.

criticalViews.summary: Because the novel was cut away from a farce about Siamese twins, and the seams show, an older critical line holds that its power is accidental and its structure a wreck: the Capellos are vestigial, the tone lurches, and the ending is hurried.
criticalViews.counter: The seams are also the method. A book about people whose identities are assigned by accident is not obviously harmed by having been assembled from another one.

criticalViews.summary: Read alongside Conan Doyle, Wilson is a scientific detective whose method, fingerprints, was newer than anything in Baker Street; the trial chapters are a courtroom drama built to the pattern later fiction made standard.
criticalViews.counter: The detection solves the crime and settles nothing: the innocent man is ruined and the guilty one sold, so the genre’s satisfaction is deliberately withheld.

essayQuestions.question: ‘Training is everything.’ How far does the novel believe its own maxim?
essayQuestions.focus: Nature, nurture and the evidence on both sides
plan: Start with the experiment itself: two babies told apart only by their clothes, exchanged in Chapter 3.
Use Chapter 4 to show what training produces, a petted tyrant and a loyal servant, and note that Tom is already ‘a bad baby’.
Take Chapter 10 as the test: Tom’s ‘moral landscape’ changes and then, within a week, settles back.
Set Roxy’s speech in Chapter 14, blaming his cowardice on his blood, against the narrator’s own explanations.
Finish with the Conclusion, where training proves permanent for Chambers and the maxim is both vindicated and made unbearable.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the role of the Calendar maxims in The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson.
plan: Establish what the Calendar is inside the story: the almanac that proves to the town Wilson is a fool.
Show how a maxim reads differently before and after its chapter, using ‘the annoyance of a good example’ above the murder.
Trace the run of dogs, from the half-dog joke to the starving dog, as the Calendar’s commentary on property and gratitude.
Consider the maxims that seem unrelated to their chapters, and whether their coldness is the point.
End with the Conclusion’s ‘more wonderful to miss it’ as the book’s final judgment on its own country.

essayQuestions.question: How does Twain present Roxy?
plan: Begin with the description in Chapter 2: majestic, white to the eye, a slave by one part in sixteen.
Read her reasoning in Chapter 3 as argument rather than instinct, precedent by precedent.
Mark the turn in Chapter 8, where the narrator describes her frame straightening as she stops begging.
Use Chapter 14 and Chapter 16 to weigh her contempt for cowardice against the son who sells her.
Decide whether the Conclusion, with her spirit quenched, punishes her or mourns her.

essayQuestions.question: ‘The fingerprints prove who did it, and the town decides what it means.’ Discuss the ending.
essayQuestions.focus: Evidence, law and the limits of detection
plan: Describe Wilson’s method in Chapter 21 and what it can actually establish: that a hand is a hand.
Show how the courtroom attaches to that hand a name, a race and a legal status the prints cannot carry.
Examine the creditors’ argument in the Conclusion as a piece of reasoning the narrator calls reasonable.
Compare the fates of Tom and Chambers, and ask what the verdict restores to either.
Conclude on whether the book is a detective story with a tragic ending or a tragedy that uses a detective.

discussionQuestions: Percy Driscoll spares his slaves and records his mercy in his diary. What does the scene say about how the town understands kindness?
Chambers has almost nothing to say for himself. Why does Twain give the real heir so small a voice?
The twins were left over from a farce. Do they belong in this novel, and what would be lost without them?
Judge Driscoll is a judge who despises going to law. Is the Virginia code presented as noble, absurd, or both?
The town names Wilson a pudd’nhead and keeps the name for twenty years. What does the novel suggest about how reputations are made and unmade?

related.why: The same river and the same institution a decade earlier, told by a boy who does not understand what he sees; this book is the same subject with no boy and no comedy.
Twain’s first Missouri river town, where the same cats sleep on the same windowsills and the slaves are almost invisible.
The novel that made ‘sold down the river’ a national phrase, and whose reformer’s confidence Twain’s ending answers with a governor’s pardon.
Slavery described from inside it by a man who escaped; Roxy’s account of the Arkansas plantation in Chapter 18 belongs beside it.
Detection by physical evidence, published within a few years of Wilson’s fingerprints, and equally sure that the body cannot lie.
